name: Handle dangerous goods shipments
function: LTL terminal operations and safety compliance
summary: About one LTL shipment in twenty contains dangerous goods such as paints, solvents, aerosols, batteries or corrosive cleaners. Federal Transportation of Dangerous Goods rules require a correct shipping document that travels in the cab, labels on the packages, placards on trailers above 500 kg, segregation from incompatible freight and a training certificate for everyone who handles them. Drivers, dock workers and dock supervisors repeat these checks at pickup, the origin dock, the hub and the destination, and missing paperwork or a leaking package stops the shipment.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian LTL and truckload carrier of about 3,000 employees with 38 LTL terminals, five hub cross-docks, a TMS with handheld scanning and a separate document imaging system.
baseline.notes: One case is one dangerous goods shipment from pickup to delivery. Step times are the dangerous-goods work added to normal handling, which is counted in the dock and delivery workflows.

trigger: A shipper tenders a shipment with a dangerous goods shipping document at pickup.
end_state: The shipment is delivered with its document retained, or it is refused, returned or held after a release has been reported.

volume.seasonality: Paints, coatings and pool chemicals rise in spring; heating fuels and de-icing products in autumn.

evidence.note: Agrees with the organisation file: about 5% of 150,000 monthly LTL shipments; share is the author's estimate.
DG checks at pickup and delivery spread over many city drivers. Author's estimate.
Certified dock workers at the 38 terminals. Author's estimate.

roles.title: Hub dock worker and forklift operator

evidence.note: Certified hub dock workers. Author's estimate.
Compatibility and placard decisions at origin and hub. Author's estimate.
DG data entry, document filing and holds. Author's estimate.
Document and placard checks before departure; not listed for this process in the organisation file. Author's estimate.
Calls to shippers about faulty documents; not listed for this process in the organisation file. Author's estimate.
Release assessments and reports; the rest of the two specialists' time is training and audits. Author's estimate.

systems.name: Transportation management system (LTL and truckload operations, billing, rating)
Document imaging for bills of lading and delivery receipts
Linehaul load planning tool and planning spreadsheets
Electronic logging devices and telematics platform
Email, phone system and contact centre software
Safety management system (driver files, collisions, roadside inspections)

steps.name: Check the shipping document and labels at pickup
steps.description: At the shipper's dock the city driver reads the dangerous goods shipping document (UN number, shipping name, class, packing group, quantity, 24-hour number and the consignor's certification), checks that the packages carry matching labels and are not leaking, and puts the document in the cab pouch within reach. A missing or incomplete document is grounds to refuse the freight.

error.defect_description: Driver accepts a document with a wrong UN number or missing 24-hour number.

control.basis: TDG Regulations Part 3: consignor completes the shipping document before the carrier takes possession; copy kept within the driver's reach

evidence.note: Shipping document contents, location in the cab and the carrier's right to refuse from Transport Canada; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Get the shipper to correct the document
steps.description: The driver calls the city dispatcher, who phones the shipper's contact to have the document corrected or reprinted while the driver waits or moves to the next stop and returns; if it cannot be fixed the freight stays with the shipper.

evidence.note: Carrier may refuse or ask the consignor to comply (Transport Canada shipping document bulletin); shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Hand the DG documents to the dock at the terminal
steps.description: Back at the terminal the driver hands the dangerous goods documents to the dock supervisor or drops them in the DG tray before the trailer is unloaded, so the dock knows which pieces need special handling.

evidence.note: Wait is the rest of the pickup route; author's estimate.

steps.name: Key the DG details into the TMS
steps.description: The terminal service clerk enters the UN numbers, classes, packing groups and quantities from the document into the shipment record, which sets the DG flag the load planners and dock see.
outputs: DG flag and details in TMS

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian LTL dangerous goods practice.

steps.name: Check DG packages as they are unloaded
steps.description: A certified dock worker unloads the dangerous goods pieces, checks labels and marks against the document, looks for leaks, damage or wet packaging and sets them in the DG staging area away from food and incompatible freight.

control.basis: TDG Regulations s. 6.1: only a person holding a valid TDG training certificate, or working under the direct supervision of one, handles or transports dangerous goods

next.condition: document and packages do not match

evidence.note: Training certificate rule from the TDG training bulletin; minutes are the extra DG handling over a normal unload, author's estimate.

steps.name: Check compatibility for the outbound trailer
steps.description: The dock supervisor looks at the other dangerous goods and food loads planned for the outbound trailer and uses the company segregation chart to keep incompatible classes apart (for example oxidizers away from flammable liquids, poisons away from foodstuffs), choosing the trailer and position.

control.basis: Company DG segregation chart (based on the US 49 CFR segregation table for cross-border loads)

evidence.note: Segregation tables not opened; practice described from general knowledge of carriers running into the US.

steps.name: Load and secure the DG freight
steps.description: A dock worker loads the dangerous goods at the chosen position, usually near the tail for access, blocks and braces it so it cannot shift, and scans it onto the trailer.

control.basis: TDG Regulations s. 6.1: only a person holding a valid TDG training certificate, or working under the direct supervision of one, handles or transports dangerous goods

evidence.note: Certificate rule from the TDG training bulletin; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Decide whether the trailer needs placards
steps.description: Before the trailer closes the dock supervisor totals the gross mass of dangerous goods on it by class and checks the exclusions (ERAP goods, certain classes) to decide whether primary class placards, a DANGER placard or none are required.

error.defect_description: Placards omitted when the total exceeds 500 kg.

control.basis: TDG Regulations s. 4.15 placards on each side and end; s. 4.16.1 500 kg exemption and its exclusions

evidence.note: Placarding rules from Transport Canada; share of trailers over 500 kg is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Apply placards to the trailer
steps.description: A dock worker fixes the required placards on both sides and both ends of the trailer, with the UN number where the goods need an ERAP.

evidence.note: Placard positions from Transport Canada; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Prepare the DG manifest and document envelope
steps.description: The dock supervisor prints the trailer's dangerous goods list from the TMS, puts the shipping documents in the envelope for the linehaul driver and confirms the DG details on the load record the linehaul planners use.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian LTL dangerous goods practice.

steps.name: Linehaul driver checks documents and placards
steps.description: Before hooking the trailer the linehaul driver checks that the DG envelope matches the manifest and that placards are in place, and keeps the documents within reach in the cab for the trip.

control.basis: TDG Regulations Part 3: shipping document within the driver's reach during transport

evidence.note: Location of the shipping document in the cab from Transport Canada; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Unload and recheck DG freight at the hub
steps.description: At the hub cross-dock a dock worker unloads the DG pieces, checks labels and condition again and moves them to the outbound door, keeping incompatible classes apart in staging.

control.basis: TDG Regulations s. 6.1: only a person holding a valid TDG training certificate, or working under the direct supervision of one, handles or transports dangerous goods

evidence.note: Transit from origin terminal to hub of 4 to 15 hours; author's estimate.

steps.name: Reload with segregation at the hub
steps.description: The hub dock worker loads the pieces on the outbound trailer at a position the hub supervisor has checked for compatibility, blocking and bracing them.

control.basis: TDG Regulations s. 6.1: only a person holding a valid TDG training certificate, or working under the direct supervision of one, handles or transports dangerous goods

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian LTL dangerous goods practice.

steps.name: Recalculate placards and documents for the outbound trailer
steps.description: The hub dock supervisor totals the DG on the new trailer, decides on placards, updates the manifest and moves the shipping documents into the new envelope.

error.defect_description: Placard decision or document transfer wrong on the outbound trailer.

evidence.note: Placarding rules from Transport Canada; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Unload and stage DG freight at the destination terminal
steps.description: At the destination terminal a dock worker unloads the DG pieces, checks them and stages them for the city route, keeping the shipping documents with the freight.

control.basis: TDG Regulations s. 6.1: only a person holding a valid TDG training certificate, or working under the direct supervision of one, handles or transports dangerous goods

evidence.note: Linehaul transit of 4 to 24 hours; author's estimate.

steps.name: City driver checks document and labels before the route
steps.description: At the start of the shift the city driver confirms that the DG document for each DG shipment on the trailer is in the cab pouch and that the trailer needs no placards for what it carries.

control.basis: TDG Regulations Part 3: document within the driver's reach

evidence.note: Document location rule from Transport Canada; wait is overnight staging, author's estimate.

steps.name: Deliver and return the DG paperwork
steps.description: After delivering the shipment the driver returns the shipping document copy with the signed delivery receipt at the end of the route.

evidence.note: Wait covers the route until the stop and the return to the terminal; author's estimate.

steps.name: File the shipping document for two years
steps.description: The terminal service clerk scans the shipping document with the delivery receipt into imaging so a copy can be produced for an inspector for at least two years.

control.basis: TDG Regulations s. 3.11: carrier keeps a copy of the shipping document for at least two years

evidence.note: Two-year retention for consignor, carrier and importer.

steps.name: Isolate and contain a leaking package
steps.description: Two certified dock workers clear the area, put on gloves and goggles, overpack the leaking package or contain the spill with the spill kit following the emergency guide, and keep other freight away.

control.basis: Terminal spill response procedure and TDG training for handlers

evidence.note: Spill handling with two people is the author's estimate of common terminal practice.

steps.name: Assess the release and make the required reports
steps.description: The dangerous goods specialist is called, reads the shipping document, phones the 24-hour number, decides against the quantity table whether the release must be reported to CANUTEC, local authorities and the consignor, and decides whether the freight can continue once overpacked or must go back.

control.basis: TDG Regulations Part 8: emergency report above the quantity table (s. 8.2) and release report to CANUTEC and the consignor (s. 8.4)

next.condition: returned to the shipper or disposed; release recorded
reportable release needing a follow-up report

evidence.note: Reporting rules and thresholds from Transport Canada; shares and minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Write the 30-day follow-up report
steps.description: For a reportable release the specialist drafts the 30-day follow-up report on form TP16-0086 with the quantities, cause and corrective actions, and files it.

evidence.note: Follow-up report form named by Transport Canada; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Hold the shipment and get a corrected document
steps.description: When the packages and the document do not match, the service clerk holds the shipment in the DG area and asks the shipper, through customer service or directly, for a corrected document before it can move.

control.basis: TDG Regulations Part 3: shipment does not move without a compliant shipping document

evidence.note: Undisclosed dangerous goods may be warehoused at the consignor's expense under bill of lading conditions; shares are the author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Faulty shipping document at pickup
exceptions.description: The driver will not take the freight until the shipper corrects the document; about a third stay behind.

exceptions.name: Document and packages do not match at the dock
exceptions.description: The shipment is held until the shipper sends a corrected document, usually a day or two.

exceptions.name: Leaking or damaged package
exceptions.description: Dock workers contain the package and the DG specialist decides on reports and whether the freight continues.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from pickup to delivery and filing

evidence.note: LTL transit of one to four days as in the organisation file summary; most shipments move within a region in one to two days. Author's estimate.
Certificate expires 36 months after issue for road, rail or marine.

benchmarks.unit: kg gross mass of DG in small containers

evidence.note: Exemption does not apply to ERAP goods and several classes.

benchmarks.population: Consignors, carriers and importers in Canada (TDG s. 3.11)

evidence.note: Copies may be kept electronically.

pain_points.description: Shippers tender incomplete or wrong shipping documents, which stops the freight at pickup or at the dock while someone chases a correction.

evidence.note: Carrier may refuse a shipment whose document is incomplete.

pain_points.description: Placard and compatibility decisions are repeated by hand at every terminal where the freight changes trailers.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common Canadian LTL dangerous goods practice.

pain_points.description: Only certified workers may handle DG, so freight waits when the certified person on the shift is busy, and certificates must be renewed every three years.

evidence.note: Certificate requirement and 36-month validity.

assumptions: Step times are the dangerous-goods work added to normal pickup, dock, linehaul and delivery handling; the elapsed time includes the shipment's normal transit, so the cycle time follows LTL transit times.
About 70% of DG shipments pass through a hub and 30% move directly between terminals; about 30% of trailers carrying DG exceed the 500 kg placard exemption. Author's estimates.
The segregation chart is described from general knowledge; the TDG text on segregation and the US segregation table were not opened.

linehaul-driver and city-dispatcher are added to this process; the organisation file lists hub and terminal dock workers, the DG specialist and city drivers but not the dock supervisors who make placard and compatibility decisions or the linehaul drivers who carry the documents. dock-supervisor and terminal-service-clerk are also missing from the organisation file's role list for this process.
The organisation file says the process produces DG documents for ltl-linehaul-planning; refused and returned shipments also go back to the shipper.
Loaded costs come from the organisation file (wage times 1.30 for hourly staff, 1.35 for salaried).

sources.title: TDG Bulletin: TDG Training
sources.supports: Section 6.1 training certificate for anyone who handles, offers or transports dangerous goods; untrained person only under direct supervision; certificate expires 36 months after issue for road; records kept until two years after expiry; certificate produced immediately on request.

sources.title: TDG Bulletin: Shipping documents
sources.supports: Minimum shipping document contents (UN number, shipping name, class, packing group, quantity, 24-hour number, consignor certification); copy within the driver's reach or in the door pocket; carrier may refuse a shipment whose document is incomplete; copies kept two years (s. 3.11).

sources.title: Dangerous goods placards
sources.supports: Placards on each side and each end of a large means of containment (s. 4.15); 500 kg exemption for small containers (s. 4.16.1) and its exclusions; optional DANGER placard limits (s. 4.16); UN number display for ERAP goods.

sources.title: Guide for reporting dangerous goods incidents: reports for road, rail and marine
sources.supports: Emergency report to local authorities above the quantity table (s. 8.2); release report to CANUTEC and the consignor (s. 8.4); 30-day follow-up report form TP16-0086; thresholds such as any quantity for PG I or II and 30 L or 30 kg for PG III.

sources.title: Bill of Lading Terms & Conditions
sources.supports: Canadian LTL bill of lading conditions: written notice of claim within 60 days of delivery (9 months for non-delivery), final claim within 9 months of shipment, liability of CAD 4.41 per kg for Canadian origin, undisclosed dangerous goods may be warehoused at the consignor's expense. Current version; the claim limits match the long-standing provincial uniform conditions.
